#155567. The Psychology of a Hippopotamus's Passing

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Psychology of a Hippopotamus's Passing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • According to recent reports, last week, the death of Fiona, a hippopotamus residing at the Cincinnati Zoo, resulted in a massive outpouring of grief.
  • As a member of the Cincinnati Zoo myself, I felt very sad to learn of Fiona's passing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

According to recent reports, last week, the death of Fiona, a hippopotamus residing at the Cincinnati Zoo, resulted in a massive outpouring of grief. As a Cincinnati resident, I was caught off guard by the magnitude of concern expressed not only locally but also around the world. This episode led me to ponder the psychology underlying why Fiona's death had such a profound impact.

As a member of the Cincinnati Zoo myself, I felt very sad to learn of Fiona's passing. In Cincinnati, this hippo had become a community icon. Fiona was born prematurely nearly 10 years ago, weighing about half as much as a typical newborn hippo (Cincinnati Zoo, 2026). Over the weeks that followed, the public watched zookeepers keep Fiona alive through round-the-clock monitoring in a makeshift ICU, feeding her by hand and celebrating each milestone she reached on her path to survival. When Fiona died, buildings throughout Cincinnati were illuminated in purple to commemorate her passing, and news outlets around the world covered her death and its impact.

Below, I outline several psychological processes that help to explain how this zoo animal touched so many people, both during her rise to celebrity and following her tragic and sudden death.

Anthropomorphism involves attributing human qualities to nonhuman entities, and people often anthropomorphize animals with whom they feel a close connection (McConnell et al., 2025). When people see a baby hippopotamus being bottle-fed by caregivers holding her in their laps, it evokes associations with parents caring for their own babies. Even her name, Fiona, was inspired by Princess Fiona, a character from the movie Shrek, because her fluted ears reminded zoo patrons of the animated princess (ironically, we're dealing with two layers of anthropomorphism here!).

In a recent development, as people anthropomorphize nonhuman entities, they often attribute humanlike emotional capacities to them, which can increase their moral concern and desire to care for those entities (Waytz et al., 2010). Thus, seeing similarities between Fiona being bottle-fed by zookeepers and human babies likely increased people's concern for Fiona and, consequently, intensified their grief following her death.

Moreover, the frequency with which people encountered Fiona throughout her life (e.g., numerous news updates about her progress, t-shirts and ice cream flavors featuring Fiona) may have increased their positive feelings toward her through the classic mere exposure effect (i.e., we tend to like things that become familiar to us through repeated exposure; Zajonc, 1968).

Industry observers note that one of the striking things about Fiona's introduction to the world was that she was an underdog. Fiona was premature, underweight, and needed round-the-clock care from zookeepers just to survive. In other words, Fiona faced extraordinary odds from the moment she was born.

In a recent development, people are often drawn to underdogs and root for their success. Research highlights that when individuals or groups are not expected to succeed and appear to face substantial disadvantages, people are more likely to support them in contexts ranging from Olympic competitions to geopolitical conflicts (Vandello et al., 2007). Thus, Fiona's helplessness at birth and the challenges she faced may have encouraged people to take her into their hearts and root for her survival, making her unexpected passing all the more crushing.

According to recent reports, research on parasocial relationships indicates that people can form strong emotional attachments to individuals, such as celebrities, with whom they have no direct, reciprocal relationship. Indeed, people often feel meaningful psychological connections with professional athletes, movie stars, and even fictional characters, such as those in the Harry Potter series. Research also shows that such symbolic social connections can contribute to people's sense of belonging and well-being (Gabriel & Young, 2011).

Thus, even though many people grieving Fiona's passing never visited the Cincinnati Zoo, and those who did typically only "interacted with her" from the other side of a large glass window, people experienced a genuine connection with Fiona. Consequently, they can experience meaningful grief following her unexpected death.

Moreover, when communities share emotionally significant moments, they can experience collective effervescence, powerful feelings of social connection and shared significance that can make an experience feel special or even sacred (Gabriel et al., 2020). Thus, the collective mourning of Fiona may have made her loss especially poignant while simultaneously bringing people together through their shared grief.

Fiona died on November 19, 2026, from complications after swallowing a child's knit hat that, through a freak accident, landed in her enclosure. Her death led to a surge of anger from internet commenters calling for "justice" (Contrera et al., 2026). Why couldn't people simply accept Fiona's death as a very sad and tragic accident?

One vital contributor to these feelings of anger may be counterfactual thinking, or people's tendency to imagine alternatives to events that take place. When trying to make sense of the world, people often engage in "if only" thinking to imagine how things might have turned out differently (e.g., "Would I have made my flight on time if there hadn't been an accident on the expressway?"). The unusual circumstances of a child's hat ending up in Fiona's enclosure make it especially easy to imagine alternative outcomes in which Fiona never swallowed the hat and would still be swimming in her zoo enclosure today.

Industry observers note that indeed, people often experience particularly strong negative emotions when it is easy to mentally "undo" a heartbreaking outcome. Under such circumstances, people may find it difficult to accept an outcome as simply a "bad break" or a matter of chance (Sherman & McConnell, 1996).

Sources indicate that it's not surprising that Fiona's death had such a profound impact on people, both here in Cincinnati and around the world. Yet, animals die in zoos every day with far less (and often no) public attention.

In a recent development, fiona's story illustrates how several psychological processes can converge to make an animal especially meaningful in people's lives. Anthropomorphism encourages us to extend moral concern to animals (McConnell et al., 2025), underdog narratives give us someone to root for (Vandello et al., 2007), parasocial relationships allow us to feel connected to individuals we do not personally know (Gabriel & Young, 2011), and counterfactual thinking can make an unexpected loss feel especially tragic when it seems so easily avoidable (Sherman & McConnell, 1996).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The California Department of Motor Vehicles has temporarily banned autonomous rideshare operator Waymo from operating on freeways in the Golden State.

In a recent development, the ban went into effect on November 11, and was prompted by an “imminent hazard to public safety,” according to the California DMV. The automotive regulator stated two specific incidents in which Waymo vehicles disregarded construction zones and law enforcement, pushed the ban forward, CNN reports.

The California DMV stated Waymo will remain banned until it “demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.” Specifically, the Alphabet-funded autonomous vehicle operator will have to prove that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones and emergency vehicles.

The freeway restriction applies to revenue ride-share operations, as well as test vehicles. Waymo will continue to operate normally on surface streets in its California markets. Right now, Waymo operates in Los Angeles, San Diego, and the Bay Area.

Recent findings suggest that “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” Waymo said in a statement to Road & Track. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

According to recent reports, one of the incidents that allegedly spurred this ban was caught on video earlier this month. The video shows California Highway Patrol patrol cars creating a traffic break on Interstate 280 near San Francisco while a Waymo vehicle attempts to pass through the rolling roadblock. California Highway Patrol officers quickly cut in front of the Waymo, which appears to stop the Waymo from attempting to pass again.

This is not the first time Waymo has faced scrutiny related to its highway operations. The company filed a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration earlier this year over driving software that repeatedly entered freeway construction zones. Waymo also briefly paused highway operations in San Francisco and Los Angeles this May over similar construction zone concerns, according to CNN.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially said about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

In a recent development, the issue stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota remarked the matter occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota remarked in the NHTSA report that the matter was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

Industry observers note that OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

In a recent development, other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet revealed next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage demonstrates rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been announced yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

Industry observers note that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a massive moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

It has been revealed that both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

It has been revealed that “Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

It has been revealed that “Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

Sources indicate that ISACK HADJAR HAS a problem. The 22-year-old Red Bull Formula 1 driver has finally gotten his hands on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he's slightly concerned about what that might do to his free time.

“It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. He's only managed to squeeze in about 25 minutes of gameplay so far this weekend, but his verdict is already in: “It's amazing.”.

Industry observers note that for now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight. “I'm a professional,” he says with a smirk. “When I know it's time to go to sleep, I go to sleep.”.

That level of discipline extends well beyond bedtime. In a sport that demands lightning-fast reflexes, intense concentration, and serious physical endurance, Hadjar has developed a pretty specific routine to get his brain and body ready to perform.

Recent findings suggest that take his pre-race ritual, which he has down to a science. He stretches and warms up with his trainer, including juggling and reaction-time tests to prime the brain. He listens to rap music—French, American, or British—to get himself hyped.

According to recent reports, then, exactly nine minutes before the race begins, he starts putting in his earpieces. “Not 10, not 11, nine," he indicates.

It's not a superstition or a lucky number. (That would be six, the number he drives with for Red Bull.) It’s simply what he’s found to be the perfect amount of time to get in the car and get ready to race. “I hate staying in the car doing nothing,” he claims. “So for me, nine minutes is the maximum time.”.

While he enjoys the pre-race preparation, there's one part of training he'd happily skip: zone 2 cardio, running at a moderate pace to power up his endurance.

“It’s just boring. I like conditioning more,” he says. To get through it, he puts on a movie, TV show, or music. “It goes by quickly in the end, but it's just, I feel like it's a waste of time. But it's very vital.”.

According to recent reports, when the race is over, Hadjar's routine is considerably more relaxed. A good meal helps him switch his brain off—specifically, a burger with caramelized onions, cheddar, tomato, and lettuce. He’ll also watch anime and FaceTime his parents, especially after a good result.

And now, of course, there will be GTA VI waiting for him. Whether he'll be able to stick to that bedtime routine is another question.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.
  • A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.
  • A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, upcoming data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

It has been revealed that vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

The shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” stated Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Some of these factors, Tse said, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

The vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what newly introduced or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

In a recent development, some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

It has been revealed that tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

When the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

Tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge newly introduced parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ford may be talking up the new Fathom EV as its latest “Model T moment,” but the Blue Oval arguably already had one this century, and it’s called the Maverick. The compact unibody pickup landed in 2021 with a splash worthy of Homer Simpson off a high dive, thanks to its mix of truck bed utility, car-like ride and handling, and available hybrid power, all—technically if not practically—available for under $20,000.

It has been revealed that prices have admittedly climbed since then, even outpacing inflation, and the lineup has seen its fair share of rejiggering over the last five years; the standard engine switched from the hybrid setup to the turbocharged inline-four and then back to the hybrid, for example. The biggest change, however, has been the addition of more fun variants: the off-road focused Tremor and the on-road oriented Lobo, the latter of which aims to Ouija-board the spirit of the original F-150 Lightning to the best of its front-wheel drive-based capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that but what if you already have a Maverick and want to add some zip? Or the Lobo’s just isn’t potent enough for you? Well, that’s where the new Maverick SV300T Package comes into play. But you’ll have to pony up Mustang-like money if you want to see your new compact pickup come equipped with it when you pick up your zero-mile new rig at the local Blue Oval dealer.

The package—which, regrettably, shoves the numerical portion of its name between the letters to keep it from being a proper SVT—comes from the Ford Custom Garage, Dearborn’s in-house upgrade division, and ties together official Ford Racing parts and other Ford accessories to make a sportier Maverick. It’s made for AWD XLT, Lariat, and Lobo models, with the marquee attracting an engine reflash and a Mustang EcoBoost-sourced turbo and an upgraded intercooler to push power from 250 hp and 280 lb-ft to 300 hp and 250 lb-ft; there’s also a Borla exhaust. XLT and Lariat rigs gain Maverick Lobo shocks, lowering springs, and upgraded stabilizer components; they can also opt for an available front brake upgrade. (When we tested it earlier this year on a short autocross course, we found the effects of both power and exhaust both quite noticeable, while the upgraded suspension amped up the delights in the turns.).

On top of that, Ford throws in a few visual upgrades to help make the SV300T’s presence known even before people hear that Borla exhaust. 20-inch wheels come in either black or bronze, as do matching hood and body graphics. Specific lettering on the tailgate also comes along for the ride, and XLT and Lariat trim versions pick up a new lower front spoiler. Plus, if you buy the package with a new Maverick, performance-oriented tires are included, whereas customers adding it after purchase will have to pick them out separately.

According to recent reports, choosing to get the SV300T at purchase, however, means adding $13,395 to the price of a newly introduced Lobo, and $15,595 to an XLT or Lariat. Granted, that includes installation and allows owners to wrap it into the truck’s financing, but that still pushes the price to $49,680 for the XLT and $48,090 for the Lobo, based on 2027 model year pricing. (Ford’s announcement says it’s meant for 2025 and 2026 model year trucks, but considering it also mentions that the package is available on new Mavericks, it seems highly unlikely that it would not be available for 2027 ones too.).

According to recent reports, buy SV300T à la carte instead, and the pricing seems a bit more stomach-able; the XLT kit will run you $6075, and the Lobo version $4500. Keep in mind, though, doing so means you’ll have to have an ASE-certified tech handle the install, and you’ll still need to go out and buy new rubber on top of that to make the most of it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
  • The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • In a recent development, texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

In a recent development, texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of upcoming capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

Recent findings suggest that “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” remarked Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

The article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

In a recent development, the storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

Recent findings suggest that more than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty notes the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

#155557. Never Fight a Pig? Why Sometimes You Have To

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (799 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Never Fight a Pig? Why Sometimes You Have To

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • You'll just get dirty, and the pig likes it.
  • It sounds high-minded, and it's a relief not to have to fight anyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

Never fight with a pig. You'll just get dirty, and the pig likes it.

You've heard that line. It sounds high-minded, and it's a relief not to have to fight anyone. You keep your hands clean, you deny the pig its satisfaction, and you get to mutter "pig" as you walk away.

According to recent reports, it's the same comfort as "When they go low, we go high" or "Love trumps hate." These claims soothe because they're conclusive, flattering, and easy. They take the pressure off engaging in conflict and flatter us as high, not low; loving, not hateful. We rarely kick the tires on such proud proclamations from a safe distance. We should, because they leak.

Never fight with a pig? Even a pig who harms your family, or sells your country for parts and pockets the profits? I say never say never. Sometimes you have to fight. You will get dirty, and the pig will like it, at least at first. The real question is how to make the fight less fun for the pig. Not how to strut off triumphant, but how to get a pig to stop being a pig and admit they're human.

In a recent development, here's a poke at a definition. A pig blames all of their mistakes on others, and does so with the preening pretense of God-like authority. Their logic is circular: "Since I deem everything I do perfect, I'm the supreme authority, and so qualified to deem everything I do perfect." It's the same circularity as claiming a sacred text is the word of God because the text says so.

In a recent development, that isn't "playing God" in the sense of changing the world. It's playing God by pretending you're the authority on which changes are permissible. It's the sneer at moral relativism from someone who declares their own subjective morality the last word, so anyone who challenges them is the devil.

A pig acts like they can do no wrong and so feels free to do endless wrong. They like getting dirty because, in their minds, they can't get dirty. They're sadistic narcissists, elevated through theatrical contempt for rivals. When someone contemptible dirties them, that proves they're clean.

It has been revealed that pigs are self-winding. Praise proves they're perfect. Condemnation proves they're perfect too, because they've already decided that anyone who condemns them is contemptible. Pigs don't go low. They go low from on high, nasty to anyone who triggers them yet entitled to be nasty because they've declared themselves saints.

It has been revealed that how do you yank them off their high horse without mounting it yourself? The best answer I have so far: Get comfortable being dirtied. Stop trying to win battles with them. Stop trying to get them to dismount and be nice. They're addicted to playing God, so they won't just quit.

Recent findings suggest that stop trying to win arguments, too, and stay off your own high horse. Skip the morality lectures and the fact-checking, because you can't beat them at that game. The only rule of their game is that anyone who challenges their authority is beneath contempt.

Instead, expose the game, over and over. Interpret their contempt as nothing more than the game. Point out that they'll say anything to pretend they're the authority, and when they respond as though they're the authority, thank them for proving you right.

In a recent development, I've been doing this online for a while, holding up a mirror to the game. I get thousands of responses, all true to formula. Nobody shares an opinion; they make pronouncements. Anyone who challenges their authority is dismissed from their supreme courtroom. I get called every insult in the book, over and over. It doesn't make me flinch. It's boring, a broken record preening as an unbroken one.

It has been revealed that I never defend myself, as if appealing in their courtroom. That would be enabling. I never take the bait, because they don't mean it. Their output is inconsistent nonsense on stilts, so I don't feel dirtied. I keep my own counsel on whose counsel I keep, and it isn't theirs.

I've even come to enjoy it. It's fun tangling them up in their own nonsense. They always respond with a defensive pronouncement that they are never triggered, and I tease them right back about how defensive and triggered they sound. It's a taste of their own medicine.

According to recent reports, that's all you can do, and all you need to do. You won't want to, but it's a civic duty.

WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts. What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

"All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

Sources indicate that since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move. Below, we’ve rounded up the best men’s walking shoes of the year—tested, podiatrist-reviewed, and chosen for comfort, support, and all-day wearability.

Recent findings suggest that one crucial lesson we've learned from Mendeszoon is not to focus only on shoe length when determining your ideal fit. According to him, it's equally essential to consider shoe width—much like with running shoes. Many brands now offer a range of widths, so understanding your foot anatomy is key to the right fit. "Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking.".

Recent findings suggest that once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is crucial to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," indicates Mendeszoon. Even when you're primarily sporting them for walking. Ready to step into action? The flexible knit tongue and solid heel lockdown add to the premium feel, making it a go-to for long walks, recovery days, or even light runs.

Recent findings suggest that men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita enjoyed how they felt structured, but not restrictive. Plus, Asics beefed up the outsole for better traction and longer wear. This pair will keep pace with more use. And while it's built for a neutral gait, it plays nicely with custom insoles if you need more arch support or pronation control.

Two defining features set Altra shoes apart: a roomy toe box and a zero-drop platform. This combination ensures an anatomic fit and promotes a natural gait. Your feet enjoy greater freedom to move naturally, allowing your toes to flex and bend as you walk, which encourages better biomechanics and can reduce strain on your foot's structures.

Sources indicate that compared to other Altras, the Via Olympus 2 leans more toward plush than performance. The wide-base footbed adds stability, while the rocker-shaped sole still promotes a smooth forward roll with each step—even if it’s more subtle during walking than running. That extra room in the toe box and midfoot also comes in handy during longer efforts, giving your foot space to swell without feeling cramped.

In a recent development, "I love super high stack shoes like this, and Altra’s dedication to extra-roomy toe boxes makes the Via Olympus 2 even more comfortable," notes Williams. "The rocker shape is less pronounced on my walks than when I run in them, but it’s still noticeable for turnover on each step.".

If you're planning long walks, you'll appreciate how the shoe's roomy toe box accommodates the natural expansion that occurs during extended physical activity.

Read More: Best Wide Toebox Shoes.

Fashion meets function with this shoe. It showcases a stylish design while seamlessly integrating waterproof features, exceptional durability, and a rocker bottom that ensures a buttery-smooth walking experience. It not only performs well, but looks good doing it.

It's explicitly designed for outdoor activities, making it an ideal choice for those who do most of their walking in nature. Thanks to its waterproof properties, my feet stay snug and dry, even in challenging weather conditions. Whether I'm trudging through rain-soaked paths or navigating puddles, these shoes provide unwavering protection for my feet.

Let's talk about Keen's newly patented "constant curve" construction. This design is engineered to encourage forward momentum in the wearer's stride, similar to most Hoka models. The rocker bottom facilitates a smooth transition from heel strike to toe-off, which Keen hopes can make walking more enjoyable for wearers. Based on my personal experience with these shoes, I'd say Keen has succeeded. I find myself walking faster and expending less effort, especially during long or uphill treks.

Although some reviewers have noted a rubbery off-gassing scent when the shoes are fresh out of the box, I didn't find it particularly noticeable (and I'm pretty sensitive to smells).

Read More: Best Treadmill Running Shoes.

Recent findings suggest that the Kuru Atom Trail is a purpose-built trail walking shoe designed to protect your heels, support your stride, and keep you moving confidently over rough ground. Its standout feature is the brand’s proprietary Kuru Sole, a dynamic midsole system that flexes with each step to cup and cradle the heel. Compared to traditional heel cradles, this one offers more adaptability and a locked-in feel. This is especially helpful for walkers who deal with heel pain or plantar fasciitis.

Recent findings suggest that on the trail, the Atom Trail holds its own. A synthetic upper with rugged TPU overlays adds structure and durability, while the gusseted tongue helps block out debris. The outsole is aggressive and grippy, built for varied surfaces. It’s not the lightest or most responsive option out there. Which is why we wouldn’t recommend it for trail running but rather for long hikes, uneven terrain, and daily dog walks on gravel or dirt paths; it’s an excellent pick.

Mendeszoon puts it best: "This is a true traditional trail shoe that provides great support, comfort, and protection against the elements and uneven and challenging terrain." Our only qualm is that it's a little heavy and not particularly responsive, which is why we wouldn't recommend running it. But it excels in what it's meant for—trail walking.

Bonus points: it’s made with fully vegan materials and has enough breathability to handle summer hikes without overheating your feet.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

Look for walking shoes with support and stability features labeled for your specific foot type. "Consider your foot type and [walking] gait," notes Dr. Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. "The goal is to keep your lower body in alignment as much as possible." Features such as a firm heel counter, a supportive midsole, and a secure lacing system can provide the stability you need for comfortable walking and to keep your feet properly aligned.

According to recent reports, when it comes to classification, if the shoe is stable, it is designed to help offset pronation, which is the inward rolling of the feet after landing on the ground. When a shoe is neutral, it lacks the stabilizing features, allowing your foot to fall more naturally. When a shoe is moderate, it is somewhere between those two worlds.

It has been revealed that "Cushioning absorbs shock and helps to avoid tissue irritation and damage," explains Schaeffer. It's important to choose walking shoes with sufficient cushioning to absorb impact and shock with each step. Look for shoes with cushioned insoles and midsoles made from materials like foam or gel to ensure a comfortable walking experience, especially for longer walks or on hard surfaces.

Decide if you prefer soft cushioning for impact absorption and comfort or a more responsive feel. Some shoes offer a balance between the two, so choose based on your preferences and walking style.

In a recent development, if you're in the market for a walking shoe to take you long distances frequently, be sure the models you're considering are relatively lightweight. Unless we're talking about a stability or trail shoe, which feature additional materials for added durability and support, that means under 11 ounces.

According to recent reports, pay attention to the upper material of the walking shoes, as it can impact comfort, breathability, and durability. Opt for shoes with breathable and flexible uppers made from materials like mesh or knit fabric to help keep your feet cool and comfortable. Additionally, keep an eye out for features like padded collars and tongues for even more comfort and support.

Industry observers note that I’m a certified strength and conditioning specialist based in New York and a fitness writer who loves trying the latest gear and raving to my loved ones about his latest discoveries. I have a dog, and I take him for walks twice a day. I also trek through the city from Queens to Manhattan five to six times per week. I have a pretty full roster of clients that I see in-person for training sessions and hit about 15,000 to 20,000 steps per day. Needless to say, I am on my feet A LOT, so I need to be on top of my game when it comes to comfy footwear.

I also got some assistance from Men’s Health fitness editors and medical advisors. We spent months of testing and researching to create this guide. Over the past few years, we’ve logged miles in more than 40 pairs of walking and running shoes from top brands like Asics, Hoka, Brooks, On, and more. Led by Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM and Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, along with expert input from podiatrists Schaeffer and Mendeszoon, we evaluated each shoe for fit, comfort, cushioning, support, durability, and value. We also considered real-world feedback from testers who wore these shoes during daily walks, commutes, and all-day wear.

From minimalist trainers to max-cushioned picks, we curated this list to meet a variety of foot types, walking styles, and comfort preferences—so you can find the pair that’s right for your stride.

Recent findings suggest that understanding your foot type is essential for finding the right walking shoes that offer optimal comfort and support. There are three primary arch types based on arch height: neutral, high, and flat. To determine your arch type, you can start with a simple "wet test," Mendeszoon recommends. Wet your feet and stand on a surface like concrete, sand, or a flattened paper bag. Examine the imprint left by your foot.

If your foot leaves a complete, flat imprint, you likely have low arches and would benefit from arch support or stability shoes. If the imprint indicates the heel, outer side of the foot, ball of the foot, and toes, but not the arch, you might have a neutral or high arch.

Industry observers note that while the wet test provides a basic idea, factors such as weight, biomechanics, and overall fitness also help determine your arch type accurately. For a more detailed analysis, consider visiting a local chiropractic clinic, podiatry practice, or high-quality running shoe store. Some locations offer foot scans that provide intricate information about your feet and arches.

It has been revealed that todd Sinett from Tru Whole Care in New York highlights a special machine called the Foot Levelers Digital Foot Scanner, which identifies specific pressure points on your feet that could be linked to back pain. This advanced tool offers precise measurements for customized orthotics, ensuring tailored support for your unique foot structure.

Sources indicate that yes, running shoes can absolutely be worn for walking, according to Mendeszoon. In fact, they may offer some added benefit compared to conventional walking shoes.

Running shoes are designed to absorb the impact of running, which means they can also provide good shock absorption when walking. Many people choose to wear running shoes for walking because of added support and flexibility, too.

One downside: Running shoes tend to be heavier and less breathable than walking shoes because of their more durable design. So, it's notable to note that they may not be the best choice for long-distance walking.

Recent findings suggest that it's important to replace your walking shoes regularly to ensure adequate support and cushioning, probably more frequently than you think. As a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to replace walking shoes every 300 to 500 miles (or every 3 to 5 months for those who walk for at least 45 minutes at least 3 times per week).

The specific lifespan of a shoe depends on several factors, including the frequency and intensity of use, the shoe's quality, and the type of surface you typically walk on. There are a few signs to look out for that may indicate it's time to replace your shoes:.

Ultimately, it's crucial to listen to your body and pay attention to any signs of discomfort or pain when walking. If you notice any of the above signs, it's a good idea to start looking for a new pair of walking shoes.

Recent findings suggest that powerlifting legend Mark Bell is a huge fan of walking for weight loss, as is Will Smith. This guy lost 60 pounds with walking and bodyweight workouts. And this guy lost 200 pounds by walking and eating a CICO diet. It's all about starting to add to your daily step count, and really sticking with it.

According to recent reports, "Starting slow and working your way up is better than overdoing it and giving up," Chris Gagliardi, a certified personal trainer at the American Council on Exercise, previously told Men's Health. An easy way to approach it: Commit to a quick 10-minute walk after dinner, and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable with daily movement.

It has been revealed that step counting also helps. "If you’re only getting 3,000 steps on a typical day, don’t try to get 10,000 steps the next day. That can be really discouraging. Aim for 5,000 every day for a week. Then go up to 7,000 the next week," walking coach Michele Stanten, founder of MyWalkingCoach.com and author of The Walking Solution, previously told Men's Health.

#155555. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2208 w)
📖 Baca

How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay.
  • It has been revealed that over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture.
  • Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

It has been revealed that over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” states Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

Recent findings suggest that in the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, notes physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

The term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” says Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”.

In a recent development, in the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” claims Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” says Ritchey.

If you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she notes.

Industry observers note that there's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she notes. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own prepares for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”.

In a recent development, if you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

Industry observers note that according to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” notes Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”.

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Sources indicate that because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

It has been revealed that ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she states. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”.

Sources indicate that it’s notable to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

Sources indicate that that’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”.

Sources indicate that in other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

What’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”.

According to recent reports, ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

“It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey says. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”.

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

In a recent development, beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”.

Of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” notes Girard.

Industry observers note that so if you’ve been curious to try a upcoming sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”.

According to recent reports, as the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most notable ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” claims Ritchey.

In a recent development, have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The crucial thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” claims Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

Industry observers note that they can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”.

Industry observers note that appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Industry observers note that natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the New School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

It has been revealed that kristine Thomason is a writer and editor with over a decade of experience creating content for print and digital publications. She holds a journalism degree from New York University, and is certified in personal training by the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

#155551. Medical Sharenting: Who Owns a Child's Medical Story?

Medical Sharenting: Who Owns a Child's Medical Story?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Industry observers note that my medical story became newsworthy before it became mine.
  • They wanted me to have the opportunity to experience as normal a childhood as possible and the chance to decide for myself when, how, and whether to share my medical story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Industry observers note that my medical story became newsworthy before it became mine. In 1978, after pioneering cardiac treatment as a baby, my parents were asked whether they would allow media coverage of my case. They declined.

They wanted me to have the opportunity to experience as normal a childhood as possible and the chance to decide for myself when, how, and whether to share my medical story.

The world my parents navigated was very different from the one children grow up in today. Over the last 50 years, social media has transformed how families share personal information. Yet, as someone who grew up with a serious congenital heart condition and depended on pioneering treatment to survive, I have become increasingly uneasy about the rise of medical sharenting.

Industry observers note that most parents now share information about their children online, often creating digital footprints long before children are old enough to consent. When those posts focus on a child's diagnosis, treatment, disability, or other health experiences, the practice is often described as medical sharenting. For children with serious health conditions, this can include hospital photographs, surgical updates, fundraising campaigns, and awareness activities.

Industry observers note that often, this sharing comes from a place of love. Parents may be seeking support, documenting an extraordinary journey, raising awareness, fundraising, or connecting with other families facing similar challenges. Yet, what happens when a child's medical story becomes public before they have had the chance to understand it, let alone choose how it should be told?

It has been revealed that as we grow up, we develop a sense of who we are and how we wish to be known by others. Medical sharenting can unintentionally remove a child's opportunity to decide what parts of their story they wish to share and with whom. While most parents act with the best of intentions, children are rarely involved in these decisions and are often too young to understand their implications or provide meaningful consent.

According to recent reports, children with serious health conditions are often at the centre of decisions made by others. Yet the child's own voice can easily become lost. As we place increasing importance on children's rights in healthcare, perhaps we should also ask how those principles apply to sharing their medical stories online.

A few years ago, I requested my childhood cardiac records. Having undergone pioneering treatment and spent much of my childhood in hospital, I wanted to better understand the events that had shaped my life. Instead, I discovered that records covering the first 18 years of my care had been destroyed.

Industry observers note that the irony was not lost on me. While some children today may grow up with every medical event documented online, many adults from earlier generations are discovering that their histories have disappeared altogether. Children have rarely had much say over how their medical stories are recorded or told. Both experiences raise the same question: Who owns a child's medical story?

Recent findings suggest that I am still grieving the loss of those records. They helped explain the years I was too young to remember. At the same time, I cannot imagine what it would feel like to discover that every operation, complication, hospital admission, and vulnerable moment from my childhood had been preserved online for anyone to read. The choice should not be between losing your medical history altogether and surrendering it to the public domain.

Sources indicate that growing up, I spent years trying not to be defined by my heart condition. Like many young people with chronic illness, I wanted to fit in. Children with health conditions are often vulnerable to bullying, exclusion, misunderstanding, and unwanted attention. As a result, many become cautious about disclosure and selective about who they trust with personal information.

As a teenager, a close family member offered to photograph me following major surgery so others could understand what I had been through. I declined. I did not want my illness to become the lens through which people saw me. Only much later did I begin speaking publicly about my experiences. Importantly, those were my choices, made when I felt ready and under my control.

Sources indicate that thankfully, today we are far more comfortable talking openly about health and disability, which is largely a positive development. However, there is a profound psychological difference between choosing to disclose personal experiences and discovering that someone else has disclosed them for you. Although research on medical sharenting remains limited, broader sharenting research suggests that some young people experience embarrassment, loss of privacy, and a sense of reduced control when personal information is shared online without their consent.

Parents and caregivers understandably seek support when navigating a child's illness. However, when these experiences are shared publicly, children may later encounter narratives that emphasise the impact of their condition on those around them. For some, particularly those already struggling with guilt or dependency, this may contribute to feelings of being a burden. For some, particularly those already struggling with guilt, dependency, or feeling different from their peers, this may become woven into their sense of self.

It has been revealed that A diagnosis may be part of someone's story, but it should never become the whole story. Children are more than patients, and future adults deserve the freedom to decide for themselves how their experiences are understood, remembered, and shared.

Recent findings suggest that from a psychologically informed perspective, children's health information forms part of an emerging life story. We need to look beyond the immediate benefits of sharing and consider whether it preserves the future adult's right to decide how their story is told.

Sources indicate that balancing these concerns with parents' need for support, families' need for connection, and the importance of awareness is not always straightforward. However, a useful starting point is to share the minimum information necessary, seek assent from older children where possible, and consider whose interests a post is really serving.

Before posting, it may be worth asking:.

Recent findings suggest that my parents were once asked whether they would allow my medical story to be shared publicly. They mentioned no, and in doing so they left that decision for me to make many years later. As conversations about medical sharenting continue, we need to honestly reflect on whether we are telling a child's story for them, or preserving their right to tell it for themselves.

Walrave M, Verswijvel K, Ouvrein G, Staes L, Hallam L and Hardies K (2022) The Limits of Sharenting: Exploring Parents’ and Adolescents’ Sharenting Boundaries Through the Lens of Communication Privacy Management Theory. Front. Educ. 7:803393. doi: 10.3389/feduc.2022.803393.
