📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cincinnati Zoo’s most famous resident Fiona the hippo has died at age 9.

Recent findings suggest that “We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike remarked in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore. Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore. She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”.

Recent findings suggest that last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remained stuck in her digestive track. She had undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that highlighted intestinal bunching, indicating her body was trying and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests. Just yesterday, on November 18, the zoo shared a upcoming approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers.

It has been revealed that “Fiona was such a gift,” said Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”.

Recent findings suggest that fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My most enduring professional memories of the Aughts are as follows: (1) Driving a Porsche Carrera GT with Walter Röhrl. (2) Being constantly harangued by German auto engineers about the absolute superiority of diesel engines. (3) Hyperextending my neck while driving the Grave Digger monster truck. And (4) listening to Audi rhapsodize about its obsession with the quality and feel of its switchgear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

With two decades’ distance from that time, here is my assessment of the above: (1) Sick! Peak experience. Could have probably just stopped after this and been satisfied. (2) The German auto engineers were wrong, although it took a gargantuan scandal, the expenditure of many fortunes, and the threat of a diesel-powered Audi R8 for the evangelists to finally accept the truth. (3) That hurt a lot, but I also ripped the door off the truck on a landing, so call it even. (4) I might have scoffed at Audi’s fixation at the time, but in the touchscreen world we now live in, I miss those switches and knobs. So much so, in fact, that I would happily hear again about the organization’s knob-research department.

It has been revealed that and so, as I stood out in the California sunshine on a recent day, listening to the Audi CEO, Gernot Döllner, positively geek out over the switchgear and beautifully designed accoutrements of the organization’s latest Nuvolari supercar, it was a most comforting flashback. Seriously, the man clearly relished dragging a fingernail over the aluminum air vents inside the car and listening to them ring. The lever to adjust the vent is a fully realized and glorious device. Yes, I do understand how ­ridiculous that statement sounds. But this is an exquisitely rendered piece of aluminum operating so smoothly and consistently that your brain assumes you are in the presence of quality. You can’t help it. It’s biology! Inside and out, the car is peppered with these small, beautiful delights.

And yes, the Nuvolari is almost entirely a Lamborghini Temerario under its spare, Bauhausian skin. And yes, the limited-edition Nuvolari costs over $300,000 more than the Lambo, which, to a sensible human, makes no sense. But it is a marvelous thing to behold and touch. It’s a statement of intent from Audi to return the firm’s focus to design and quality in general (as well as in switchgear and trimmings specifically). Let the rhapsodizing begin again. I’m here for it. Again.

Recent findings suggest that please enjoy this problem’s look into the Aughts, a decade that fundamentally changed cars and the culture around them. And check out the site for additional Aughts-worthy content, including a forthcoming comparison test of two V-12 ultraluxury sedans. Remember sedans?

Recent findings suggest that daniel Pund was named Road & Track's editor-in-chief in 2024 after helping to re-invent the venerable magazine brand as executive editor. For around 30 years, Pund has toiled away as a feature writer, car reviewer, editor, and columnist for every car magazine that matters (including Car and Driver and Autoweek) and a few that didn’t. He’s also contributed to Esquire and GQ and other general-interest publications.

How to Survive the Holidays With "Ignorant" Relatives

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • One phrase that changed my life forever is: "The map is not the territory.".
  • There is a reality out there—the territory—but our only way to access it is through the representations of it we create and carry around in our heads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

One phrase that changed my life forever is: "The map is not the territory.".

There is a reality out there—the territory—but our only way to access it is through the representations of it we create and carry around in our heads. These are our maps. And every human being has a slightly different map. When I say "red," and you imagine red, how can we be certain we're imagining the same hue, tint, etc.? We can't.

So, we arrive at a dining table this holiday season convinced that our opinions simply describe what any reasonable and rational person would see when they looked at the world... the facts... the territory. Naturally, a relative who disagrees with our map must be missing some vital information, or be lacking in the intelligence needed to process that information correctly, or both. We think that they are ignorant; if they only had a map as good as ours, they would agree with us.

In Role Mate to Soul Mate, relationship expert Warren Farrell writes that certainty can close us off to other people’s perspectives. His chapter “From Civil War to Civil Dialogue” offers tools for staying in conversation when disagreements get heated.

Farrell recommends preparing before the meal. Start with “nemesis visualization”: Picture the relative who interrupts, misunderstands you, or repeats their point more loudly. The goal isn’t to rehearse a fight. It’s to let go of the hope that this time you’ll finally change their mind and choose peace instead.

In a recent development, another tool is “Alone Power”: the ability, on your own, to help another person feel heard. That doesn’t mean agreeing. It means listening closely enough that the other person can see that you are truly trying to understand them. Holiday dinners put this skill to the test; we may say we want less division, while quietly hoping everyone will come around to our view. First, we need to know how to make other people feel heard.

According to recent reports, next, think of a few qualities you genuinely respect in that relative and recognize in yourself. Farrell calls attention to three possible points of common ground: caring, curiosity, and courage (the three Cs). You might not share all three, and that’s fine. Choose what resonates with you. Finding one shared quality can make it easier to stay curious about the person beneath the argument.

When the conversation starts to escalate, notice whether you’re already composing your rebuttal. Silently say “hold” to yourself, and then take a deep breath or recall something beautiful that helps you feel grounded. Try these three steps:.

Keep checking until the other person feels accurately understood.

Feeling heard often reduces someone’s need to keep arguing, so use the holidays to practice your active listening skills.

Industry observers note that this is my favorite exercise. Farrell’s premise is that a virtue, pushed to an extreme, can become a vice. The exercise asks you to look for the value inside an opinion that irritates you. In his example, a conservative father and liberal daughter discover shared values beneath their political disagreement, including compassion, equality of opportunity, and self-respect. From there, they can replace proselytizing with a search for mutual solutions.

Industry observers note that we don’t have to abandon our convictions or pretend to agree with our relatives; we simply have to become sufficiently curious to inquire why the maps in their heads are so different from the maps in ours. We can ask what matters to them, and if the conversation becomes disrespectful or frustrating, we can set a limit: “I care about you, but I don’t want to keep arguing about this. Let’s talk about something else.”.

We have to be the change we want to see in the world. Imagine how much more peaceful the world would be if we all remembered that the map is not the territory. We would waste less time believing that other people are ignorant and spend more time becoming curious about their maps. At the end of the day, everyone just wants to feel heard, seen, respected... loved. Maybe a more harmonious, compassionate, and less polarized world starts at your dining room table this holiday season.

Farrell, W. (2024). Role Mate to Soul Mate: The Seven Secrets to Lifelong Love. BenBella Books.

Breaking: Newly introduced Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued upcoming guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.
  • The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.
  • Under the upcoming guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued upcoming guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.

The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.

Under the upcoming guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.

Advances in MRI technology and biomarker testing may also help doctors determine which men need further testing, potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment.

The ACS last updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines in 2010, when conflicting research findings raised questions about whether the benefits of PSA screening outweighed the potential harms.

At the time, the organization emphasized informed, shared decision making between patients and healthcare professionals.

However, longer-term follow-up studies have since provided stronger evidence of the benefits of early detection, prompting the ACS to conduct a systematic review and patch its recommendations.

The authors of the report noted, “In making these recommendations, we recognize that PSA testing is only the first step in a screening cascade that includes secondary testing of men with an elevated PSA level and treatment decisions for men diagnosed with prostate cancer.”.

The newly introduced guidelines recommend a PSA test every 2 years for men ages 50–69 with an average risk of prostate cancer.

The recommendation for those at high risk is a PSA test every year starting at age 45.

In a recent development, for men ages 70–74, the ACS recommends individualized decision making. If an individual chooses to be screened, the ACS recommends a PSA test every 2 years until the age of 74.

Ramkishen Narayanan, MD, Director of the Center for Urologic Health at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline that screening shouldn’t automatically be ruled out for men over 75.

“[A] point worth noting is that for men over 75, their PSA history as well as their individual clinical scenarios should be evaluated, and that PSA should not be discouraged in this group of men if their life expectancy and clinical history warrant a PSA check.”.

According to the ACS, approximately 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime.

Individual risk depends on age, race/ethnicity, and other factors:.

Prostate cancer diagnoses in the United States increased by around 3% per year between 2014 and 2022, according to the ACS.

The rise in diagnoses, particularly advanced-stage prostate cancer, has renewed attention on the importance of regular screening.

“[The] current state of prostate cancer screening guidelines is vague and generalized. This has led to ambiguity, disagreement, and variation of opinion among healthcare providers and institutions in their approach to men’s health,” noted S. Adam Ramin, MD, board certified urologist, urologic oncologist, and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report.

The updated ACS guidelines drew partly on findings from a 2025 follow-up of the European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC), which found that regular PSA screening was associated with a 13% reduction in prostate cancer deaths over 23 years.

A 12-year ERSPC follow-up in 2012 also suggested that regular screening was associated with a decrease in metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis, which is another finding that influenced the updated guidance.

“Prostate cancer can take many years, even decades, to become clinically significant, so it takes a long time for us to see the consequences of changes in screening practices,” Taylor Goodstein, MD, assistant professor of urology in the College of Medicine at the University of Cincinnati, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline.

“With longer follow-up from randomized trials, we now have more convincing evidence that PSA screening reduces the risk of dying from prostate cancer,” she stated.

“The ACS guidelines are vital now because they drive home the most important point that prostate cancer screening saves lives,” noted Narayanan.

Healthcare professionals use PSA levels to help determine whether additional testing for prostate cancer may be necessary.

The ACS recommends further testing for men under 70 with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher.

For those ages 70 and older, the ACS recommends further testing if their PSA is 6.5 ng/mL or higher. This is because PSA levels tend to be naturally higher in older men.

You can speak with your healthcare professional to find out more about PSA cutoff levels.

Goodstein told Healthline that the ways this fresh guidance can change the outlook for prostate cancer are simple.

“If we screen men, we can catch troublesome cancers early, before they have a chance to spread,” she said.

Industry observers note that goodstein also emphasized how much the evaluation process has changed. In the past, an elevated PSA level often led directly to a biopsy.

Industry observers note that today, doctors generally repeat the PSA test within two weeks to three months to confirm the result. If PSA levels remain elevated, additional testing, including a prostate MRI or validated biomarker test, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary.

Narayanan told Healthline, “The fresh guidelines will hopefully remove any confusion about the value of PSA screening and encourage prostate cancer screening as an integral part of a man’s ‘checkup’.”.

He added that it is worth noting that the DRE (digital rectal exam) adds little value to the initial prostate cancer screening and is no longer something that men should fear.

“Adoption of this set of specific guidelines standardizes the approach to screening for prostate cancer. It provides a unified effort among all levels of healthcare. It most likely will increase the chances of finding prostate cancer in earlier stages and lead to improved cancer treatment outcomes,” stated Ramin.

Like the previous Elantra N, the new model will surely remain a versatile and enthralling sport sedan, complete with track-ready suspension, a rowdy exhaust note, and, most importantly, a standard six-speed manual transmission.

Expert Tip: If Hyundai does decide to bump the newly introduced Elantra N up to a higher performance bracket, it will be competing with models such as the Honda Civic Type R, Toyota GR Corolla, and Volkswagen Golf R.

Like its humble standard-matter Elantra counterpart, we think that Hyundai will give its sportiest N model a complete makeover for the 2028 model year.

#155454. Never Before in the History of Motoring: How the Splendor and Madness Of the Aughts Shaped Today’s Car World

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)

Never Before in the History of Motoring: How the Splendor and Madness Of the Aughts Shaped Today’s Car World

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it was a perfect moment.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • It felt like driving a Michigan-made Millennium Falcon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it was a perfect moment. In the driver’s seat of a 2005 Ford GT, with my best pal riding shotgun, I stared through the windshield with eyes opened as wide as the car’s headlights. The year was 2007. We were on a stretch of I-80 that dives down the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountains, from California into Nevada. The early-­morning sun hung low on the horizon in front of us. Looking out on the desert, we saw miles of empty highway, with visibility so sharp that we would see any highway patrol vehicle in our path.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

It felt like driving a Michigan-made Millennium Falcon. This Ford could hit 200 mph and beat the Ferrari Challenge Stradale around a road course. It was shamelessly retro, trading hard on the Le Mans pedigree of its GT40 ancestor, but it was also new age and American as all hell. It felt unprecedented.

Looking back now, almost 20 years later, I can see that the word unprecedented applied to the whole decade. The Aughts, defined as the years 2000 to 2009, were packed with never-before events and spectacular vehicles such as the Ford GT. It was a time of excitement and optimism, when cars were cool and quicker than ever—until it all crashed into a ditch with the economic downturn. The era was to the car industry what the Sixties were to music, politics, and assassinations. An era of profound change. Of tremendous upheaval. Of darkness and light. Of death and rebirth.

It was the decade that shaped our here and now.

On the most macro level, the Aughts were when the global automotive ecosphere began ­reordering itself into what we know today. In 2008, ­Toyota overtook GM to become the world’s largest automaker, selling 8.97 million vehicles around the world that year. The ­DaimlerChrysler partner­ship shattered. General Motors, one of the largest corporations on earth, and Chrysler, another of Detroit’s Significant Three, went bankrupt at the end of the decade, and if not for the federal government handing out bags of cash to bail out those legendary companies, they might no longer exist.

Industry observers note that GM’s Oldsmobile and Pontiac, two brands that collectively had made cars for nearly 200 years, disappeared during the Aughts. (To be fair, Pontiac did make it a few days into the fresh decade, ending production on January 4, 2010, with a last-gasp G6 sedan.) Plymouth also went bye-bye. Saturn assembled its final vehicle in 2009.

The Aughts were also the start of credible alternatives to internal-combustion motoring’s hegemony. The Toyota Prius arrived in the United States in July 2000, then became a cultural lightning rod when sales of the second-­generation model exploded in response to surging gas prices. Hybrid, a term that often applied to a kind of cannabis at the time, suddenly became lingo referring to a kind of car. At the same time, there were inklings of a lithium-ion automotive future. Tesla put out its first battery-powered car, the Roadster, in 2008, and early adopters felt the shock of a 0–60 thrust without the jolt of gears changing. Cars began to morph from machinery into the rolling computer devices that we drive today, as screens proliferated on dashboards and our phones learned to talk to our vehicles. Digital technology wormed its way deeper into every aspect of motoring, a trend that continues, albeit with far less idealism now.

The decade was a history-defining time in motorsport as well. Globally, racing saw the dawn of a latest dynastic epoch. Michael Schumacher, driving for Ferrari, claimed the Formula 1 world championship from 2000 to 2005. In large part, F1 has been a series defined by dynasties ever since. Audi and Tom Kristensen ruled Le Mans for nearly the entire decade, and for the first time, a turbo­diesel won: the R10 in 2006. In NASCAR, Jimmie Johnson took the Cup Series title five years in a row with Chevrolet starting in 2006.

Sources indicate that dynasties on this level of dominance had never happened before in any of these series. I remember sitting in a press conference after the Italian Grand Prix in 2006, when Schumacher (having just won the race) announced his first retirement. The moment he unleashed the news, he teared up and an explosion of camera flashes came from the press corps. The feeling in the room was unforgettable. What Schumacher had done during his career to that point was unprecedented.

Even pop culture had an auto­motive renaissance. The Fast and the Furious premiered on June 18, 2001, with three sequels in multiplexes before the decade was over. F&F grew into Universal Studios’ biggest film franchise and remains the most successful car-movie series ever. Pixar’s Cars came out in 2006 and became Paul Newman’s highest-grossing film, even though viewers never saw his face. Talladega Nights (also 2006) may not invite many critical superlatives, but it unapologetically roasted NASCAR, which was in on the joke. It also popularized the saying, “If you ain’t first, you’re last.” Michael Bay’s Transformers films filled theaters. There was even a Dukes of Hazzard movie with Jessica Simpson playing Daisy Duke, Burt Reynolds as Boss Hogg, and a badass General Lee Dodge Charger. Car video games saw surging popularity, sales, and advancements in graphics. The Aughts gave us Forza Motorsport, plus new and series-defining installments of Gran Turismo and Grand Theft Auto.

So much was happening in the car world that being a fan felt electrifying. The Camaro, the Charger, and the Challenger were back, and the Mustang was reborn in retro style. The first Cars & Coffee events happened in Southern California, and soon small towns around the U.S. were hosting them.

Recent findings suggest that when you throw all of this together, it made for an earth-shattering decade. Despite the dizzying news cycle, however, it was the cars themselves that we remember most. The Aughts ushered in a newly introduced era for halo cars, when automakers set out to build masterpieces that created new expectations for performance and technology. Some would say the Seventies, Eighties, and Nineties were halcyon days for car fans. But the new sheetmetal that graced our roads in the first decade of the new millennium was incomparable.

According to recent reports, ford came up with the aforementioned GT, which was the first real Ford customer supercar made in any significant numbers. Porsche gave us the Carrera GT, a mid-engine rocket ship that is one of the greatest sports cars of all time. Bugatti chased even bigger numbers with the Veyron, the first road car that could crack 250 mph and produce 1000 hp.

There were plenty of other highlights as soaring corporate confidence and unheard-of development budgets ushered in the arrival of still more icons. This was the decade of the C6 Corvette Z06 and ZR1, the Audi R8, the Ferrari Enzo, and the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren. The Bentley Continental GT and the Porsche 911 GT3 RS debuted, along with the U.S.-eligible Nissan GT-R. V-8 engines were squeezed into the BMW M3, the Cadillac CTS-V, and the Mercedes-Benz C63 AMG. It was a time of heroes.

These cars didn’t just thrill us; they were so unique and outstanding that they redefined the identities of the brands that made them and even motoring itself. That is the true legacy of the Aughts. Even if you’re too young to have lived through those years, you are reaping the rewards today. Because of all of that innovation and ambition, the future through our windshields still looks bright. But maybe a little less bright than it did back then.

Sources indicate that A.J. Baime is the author of seven books, including Go Like Hell: Ford, Ferrari, and Their Battle for Speed and Glory at Le Mans, and The Accidental President: Harry S. Truman and the Four Months that Changed the World. An R&T editor-at-large, he has driven cars on racetracks all over the U.S. and Europe, going back to 2007. He is proudly the R&T staff’s slowest track driver.

LIKE MOST SCRUFFY men, I’ve had a complicated relationship with razors. Why risk razor burn or slicing your neck for something that’s going to grow back in two days? But I’ve come to realize it’s the same reason you wear pants even though you have to clean them after. Because you don’t want to look disheveled (or denied access to restaurants). Plus, with the right technique and grooming products, one razor can give you the closest, most gentle shave possible.

Now that you’re on board with razors, it’s time to find the right tool for you. People constantly debate the best shaving method—some claim more blades give a better shave, while others argue they cause more irritation and ingrown hairs to sensitive skin. Some dudes ride for high-tech electric razors, others stand by their old-school safety razors.

As board-certified dermatologist Dr. Azadeh Shirazi, MD, puts it, there is no right or wrong answer. It comes down to personal preference and need. These are the best options for every skin type and budget.

Industry observers note that razors do not get better than Gillette's Fusion5—it’s a classic for a reason. According to celebrity hairstylist and master barber Cody Renegar, the blades are flexible enough to maintain contact with your skin at all times, while an added conditioning pad helps them glide over the skin without lifting or creating cuts. Plus, the stretchy microfin design, featuring soft and flexible horizontal fins that help stretch skin before the blades make contact, ensures a close and smooth shave.

The built-in precision trimmer, a single-edged blade positioned on the backside of the razor cartridge, also brings about a cleanly sculpted shave. This extra single blade on the top edge creates sharp detailing (like around the sideburns or mustache) without digging into your skin. Not to mention, this razor is one of the more affordable options on the market (under $6 a blade), and refills are widely available at any drugstore.

When it comes to shaving, more blades aren’t always better, but in the case of this razor, five is the lucky number. These cartridges pack in the shaving power with five blades and a larger lubrication strip, the combo of which delivers a smoother, closer shave without as much irritation.

These blades last about five shaves (one for each blade), which is a pretty good deal when compared with other, lower-priced blades that get dull faster. The handle itself is lightweight and easy to hold, with a rubberized feel that works well in the shower if you’re that kind of shaver.

Read More: Gillette Fusion 5 Review.

Sources indicate that pamper yourself with a hot towel shave using Gillette's Heated Razor. It transforms a barbershop-style shave into an at-home experience, warming the blades with chargeable, heating cartridges that soften hair as you shave.

According to recent reports, its stainless steel warming bar and flexible five-blade design work together to deliver a more comfortable, closer shave. The waterproof razor features an adjustable heat setting, letting you find your perfect temperature. Plus, it comes with a handy rechargeable stand.

It’s usually best to approach gadgets like this with a healthy dose of skepticism, and honestly, many of them don't live up to their promises. But this heated razor is one of the exceptions. In fact, it exceeds expectations. The stainless steel bar heats up to various temperatures depending on your comfort level (don’t worry, even the highest setting won’t burn your skin).

The combination of heat and five blades delivers a noticeably closer, more comfortable shave. The overall experience is smoother, and I noticed less irritation and razor burn than I usually get with non-heated razors. To be clear, at over $100 for the kit ($200 with the case), this is a luxury razor kit. But the futuristic heated design and ultra-smooth shave make it a worthwhile investment, if you can swing the price tag.

Read More: Gillette Labs Heated Razor Review.

Industry observers note that an electric razor that doesn’t pull or irritate your skin, even during the adjustment period? Yes, please. I’ve been boasting about the 100 percent waterproof Braun Series 9 Pro for years.

Sources indicate that the built-in AutoSense technology, which reads the thickness of your facial hair and automatically adjusts the power of the shaver's motor accordingly, provides a customized shave, and the ten-direction flex head makes sure to get every single spot with titanium-coated blades. Really, this is the Ferrari of razors right here—hence the price tag.

In my extensive testing of electric razors, this one stood out head and shoulders above the rest due to its tech-packed design that actually does deliver a more efficient shave, even if you have days' worth of stubble.

Industry observers note that it effectively cuts shaving time in half, and you’re able to use it both wet and dry (with or without shaving cream). However you choose to use it, if you’re thinking of making the switch to an electric shave, this is the best possible option.

This innovative electric razor shaves smoothly, cleanly, and efficiently without nicking or cutting—you can easily rub it back and forth on the skin—with long-lasting replaceable blades. While it won’t get you as close a shave as the other options on this list, it will give you a low stubble that makes you look rugged yet refined.

In fact, Dr. Penzi says that it’s the most reliable electric shaver for men prone to ingrown hairs who don’t mind maintaining some stubble. The real beauty of this electric razor-trimmer hybrid, however, is that you can use it for literally any look, anywhere you want to shave. It gives a close, clean shave on both your face and body, but also comes with length guards if you want to keep some length.

Sources indicate that the OneBlade will always be a winner because it’s so easy to use. Built like a classic razor, but with the power of an electric shave, the best thing about this device is the innovative blade, which delivers a close, fast shave with very little risk of nicking or cutting. The multiple guards allow you to customize the length of your shave.

Plus, it’s waterproof and can be used in the shower. It’s also just as effective on your body as on your face, making it an indispensable tool for all your shaving needs. Just be sure to switch the blade when using it on your body to cut down on the risk of cross-contamination of bacteria.

Read More: Philips Norelco OneBlade Review.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to beat the price of this simple yet effective razor. Dr. Garshick loves that it’s a travel-friendly razor that’s gentle on skin. It uses a soothing, lubricated strip containing aloe vera to calm the skin while giving you a close, smooth shave anywhere you use it. Best of all is the fact that you get a total of eight cartridges in this pack, making it the best value on this list.

In a recent development, disposable razors are great for certain scenarios, like travel, but they can also be pretty wasteful and, worse, not very effective. But the five-blade cartridges of this razor are equally as effective as a reusable razor with a similar design, so you’re not compromising on efficacy when choosing a disposable razor.

That being mentioned, compared to other razors on this list, the blades will get dull rapidly (after a few uses), but that’s pretty standard for a disposable.

It has been revealed that according to Dr. Shirazi, this is the perfect safety razor: It's weighted for better control, comes with a single blade to counter ingrown hairs and irritation, and has high-quality blades for a smooth shave with each stroke. Dr. Garshick also approves of Bevel's single, double-edged blade, which she notes helps to achieve a close shave without needing to apply a lot of pressure.

According to recent reports, of course, it takes a village to help limit the chances of ingrown hair and take down facial hair, so this kit has everything you need. It includes gentle shave cream, relieving post-shave balm, and 40 (!) blade refills.

It has been revealed that there is a learning curve when switching from a cartridge razor to a safety razor, so the first few times you use this razor, it’s going to take longer than you’re used to. But once you get the hang of it, including the all-important 30-degree angle, it does go faster. Though you don’t want to go too fast, as it’s easy to nick or cut yourself with this sharp, single blade.

It delivers a close shave, cutting down on the amount of ingrown hairs and post-shave irritation, which is why many people switch to a safety razor to begin with. The handle is perfectly weighted to feel hefty in your hand but still glide smoothly across your skin, making the actual act of shaving a pleasure.

In a recent development, if you have sensitive skin or are prone to irritation, shaving can become a unique form of torture. Gillette, however, has a solution. According to Dr. Shirazi, its SkinGuard razor comes with a special guard on the blade that prevents it from shaving too close but doesn’t sacrifice efficacy. It cushions every movement, eliminating tugging and helping sensitive skin stay soothed and comfortable, she says.

Sources indicate that while the two-blade design won't provide a baby-smooth shave, you can still get a pretty close cut without the rash. Besides the ease of use, Dr. Garshick also highlights the comfort of its added lubrication for an easy glide, as well as its precision trimmer for hard-to-reach areas.

Recent findings suggest that when you have sensitive skin, too many blades can destroy your face. This razor, however, just comes with two blades, plus a Skinguard feature that helps minimize how much the blades drag over your skin. The less close shave is a compromise, for sure, but it really does help protect sensitive skin from post-shave irritation. The blades are spaced out to help prevent nicks and tugs, as well—a design feature that resulted in zero (!) irritation or cuts with my first use.

In general, razors with more blades deliver a closer shave, but they also come with drawbacks. Additional blades will provide a closer and quicker shave; however, an increased risk of irritation and ingrown hairs is the tradeoff. Razors with only one or two blades are much gentler on skin, but don’t cover as much at once.

According to recent reports, these deliver a closer shave than most razors—even with just one blade—thanks to their sharp edge. That being said, these are also the most dangerous. With the wrong technique, you’re more likely to get cuts than with any other razor type.

Industry observers note that the most common razor you’ll find in any grooming aisle. Blade design plays the biggest role here—whether you use more blades or fewer. But compared to safety razors, these won’t get as close, but the risk of serious skin slicing is much lower.

Electric razors won’t give you as close a shave as blades because their heads don’t make full contact with the skin. However, they still shave close enough to keep stubble low, neat, and often unnoticeable. Dermatologist Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, recommends electric razors for people prone to ingrown hairs since they cut hair above the skin’s surface.

It has been revealed that according to dermatologist Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD, it’s important to consider the blade count, as multi-blade razors offer a closer shave, but a higher risk of irritation. While many go for a five-blade design because it'll shave faster and closer than a two-blade or one-blade (fewer strokes are needed), Dr. Shirazi argues that this can be overkill and more dangerous.

He warns that more blades can often lead to more friction and thus irritation, so it’s best to use fewer blades (no more than two) to reduce your risk of razor bumps and irritation if you have sensitive skin.

That’s not to say a single-blade design can’t also provide a close shave, if you know the right technique. If you’re prone to irritation or ingrown hairs, dermatologist Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, agrees on using razors with a single or double blade. For men with coarser, thicker hair, Dr. Penzi suggests multi-blade razors, which often deliver a closer, smoother cut with fewer strokes—reducing friction and irritation. In short, for the closest shave, go above three blades. For the gentlest shave, aim for below that number.

Industry observers note that every razor comes with its own features and strengths, because getting a clean shave is only half the battle. Before you buy, look for specs that make shaving easier and more comfortable, like handle design, waterproofing, cleaning docks, or built-in trimmers.

Sources indicate that after a few hundred strokes, or five to seven shaves, blades become dull. That said, when you're buying reusable razors, you should opt for one that has easy-to-replace refills to achieve a smooth and close shave every time. You’ll want to keep an eye on how many blades are included in the initial pack, as this will cut down on cost and how soon you’ll have to re-up after buying.

It has been revealed that we've been testing every type of razor since this article was first published in 2018. For this patch, I teamed up with fellow Men's Health editors and writers over the past year to identify which razors are right now the best-performing. Drawing from years of testing feedback and my own experience as a grooming editor and overall hairy dude, I narrowed the list down to 25 razors to trial or reevaluate. I also spoke with other grooming experts, including professional barbers and board-certified dermatologists, on which razors they recommend.

We then judged each one for effectiveness, price, ease of use, and long-term performance, as well as how frequently they caused irritation. After this research and weeks of testing each product, I landed on the seven options above as the best razors for men in 2026.

No matter what razor you use, always make sure it’s sharp (switch it after a few uses) since a dull razor will wreak havoc on your face. The most crucial thing is making sure the blade isn’t dull, as that can increase the potential for ingrowns and irritation, indicates Dr. Garshick.

According to recent reports, it’s crucial to start by wetting your face with warm water to soften facial hair, notes celebrity barber Ray Santos. "When I have time, I like to apply a hot towel directly to my skin for a few minutes before the shave to really prep my face.".

Recent findings suggest that lathering up your face with cooling shaving gel will help protect the skin from irritation. Apply it evenly over the area you plan to shave to help the blades glide smoothly across your skin, Santos says.

Industry observers note that to help prevent irritation, follow the natural direction that your facial hair grows when shaving. Keep in mind that hair doesn’t grow uniformly—what works for your cheeks might not apply to your neck or jawline, so pay attention to the grain in each area.

This includes not shaving too fast or pulling your skin taut while shaving, which will tighten the skin and give you a closer shave. But Dr. Camp warns of the latter technique's risk of razor bumps. And always shave after a shower or using a face wash when facial hair is at its softest and easiest to cut.

How Professionals May Overlook Intrafamilial Child Torture

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that intrafamilial child torture (“ICT”) usually involves a combination of physical, sexual, and psychological abuse, and intentional neglect, of a child, that is 1) severe and egregious, 2) prolonged without intervention, and 3) deliberate on the part of the offending parent (Miller, et al, 2021).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

In a recent development, coauthored with Pamela J. Miller, JD., MSW.

It has been revealed that intrafamilial child torture (“ICT”) usually involves a combination of physical, sexual, and psychological abuse, and intentional neglect, of a child, that is 1) severe and egregious, 2) prolonged without intervention, and 3) deliberate on the part of the offending parent (Miller, et al, 2021). By definition, ICT occurs within the family context and is perpetrated by someone who is considered a child's family member or caretaker.

ICT is different from most physical abuse, which is episodic and often impulsive. Most physical abuse results from parents losing control and/or accidentally hurting a child more than intended. Part of the harm of ICT is its insidious and all-encompassing nature; the child has few avenues for healthy development.

According to recent reports, while ICT is thought to be relatively rare, it's still common enough that anyone who works with children or families over a decade is apt to encounter a child who has been or is being tortured. Often, the professional will mistake the ICT for simple abuse or neglect, and will fail to offer the child meaningful assistance.

We have each seen more than a few cases of ICT over the course of our professional lives (Miller about 50, Fontes about 15). Many professionals have never heard of ICT. But even when they have, they might mistakenly discard the ICT framework if the case before them doesn’t seem to fit their idea of what ICT looks like. This can have fatal consequences.

Industry observers note that our goal here is to expand professionals’ internal schema of how ICT appears by discussing diverse presentations that we’ve encountered. This is a stand-in until research devises undoubtedly different, more robust, evidence-based typologies. We link descriptions to real cases in the popular media, so readers can learn more.

Parents who torture their children don’t necessarily lead marginal lives. They may be wealthy professionals and appear to be caring and competent in their work lives (Miller et al., 2021). Ruby Franke, a parenting influencer, appears to have tortured her children and eventually pleaded guilty to aggravated child abuse. Larry and Carri Williams were popular at their church before their convictions involving assault on one child and the death by torture of another.

While most family violence is committed by men, some ICT involves a female caregiver as the primary perpetrator. Adoptive mother Maribel Loera recently pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, concealment of a body, and multiple counts of severe child abuse, thus avoiding the death penalty. According to media reports, two of her surviving children testified to years of severe violence, including burns, beatings, and a knife attack that left permanent scars. Professionals should be aware that ICT can be driven by female perpetrators.

Some child torturers’ lives follow a pattern of abuse and withdrawal from drugs; they could be especially dangerous at any part of this cycle. They may act in extremely harmful ways when “out of their wits” from alcohol, methamphetamines, fentanyl, or other substances. However, while the substances may make episodic violence more intense or more frequent, the substances are not the cause. By definition, ICT is purposeful and deliberate.

While there is plentiful research on the higher prevalence of child abuse and neglect among caregivers who abuse substances, we were unable to find research on child torture specifically. But we’ve both seen drug-addled caretakers who seem to have lost any sense of care or morality and torture a child or children over time, sometimes fatally.

The first study to analyze a large body of ICT cases statistically (Rycus et al. 2026) found that non-biological parents are more likely to be perpetrators of ICT than biological parents. This includes stepparents, biological parents’ romantic partners, adoptive parents, foster parents, and relatives caring for children. The case of Larry and Carri Williams (mentioned above) stands out here, where parents of seven biological children adopted two children from Ethiopia, and the mother tortured the older child, Hana, until she died from malnutrition and hypothermia. While the parents used abusive punishments with their biological children, they apparently tortured only their adopted children.

Sometimes one partner (usually but not always the man in heterosexual couples) coercively controls and tortures not just one or more children, but also his adult partner. In fact, the abuser’s torture of the children may be aimed at dominating his adult partner.

Sources indicate that the abuser’s coercive control over his partner incapacitates her ability to protect the children effectively. She may try to deflect the abuser’s rage towards herself. She may sneak the children food when they are locked in the closet. Adult victims may fail to contact authorities due to a combination of fear that their children will be removed and fear that the abuser will kill them and the children before police arrive.

Sources indicate that vanity Fair reported that when the police came to arrest attorney Joel Steinberg and his girlfriend, Editor Hedda Nussbaum, for the death of their adoptive child, Lisa Steinberg, Nussbaum looked like a boxer who had sustained beatings. Nussbaum had a fractured nose and jaw, nine broken ribs, and gangrenous legs.

In some ICT cases, the parent(s) abuse all the children (e.g., the Turpins, Nixmary Brown, the family of Elisa Izquierdo). In others, the parents seem to differentiate among the children, targeting those children who are not biologically related (as in Hana Williams), who are the oldest, or who are disabled.

Many caretakers hide their tortured children from public view by homeschooling or “no- schooling” them. The under-regulation of homeschooling allows caretakers to torture children with no oversight from teachers or school officials who might otherwise make child abuse reports (Bartholet, 2020). In a typical case, the Hart parents removed their six adopted children from public school after reports of suspected child abuse. In several of the cases mentioned here, the caregivers withdrew the children from school, including the Turpin, Franke, and Williams cases.

Industry observers note that at first glance, it might seem that anyone who tortures a child is “crazy.” However, research is lacking on the possible diagnoses of caretakers who torture their children. In our experience, ICT is often perpetrated by people who show no outward signs of mental illness. People in an acute psychotic episode might kill their children, perhaps thinking that this will “save” them or because they are suffering from persecutory delusions or postpartum psychosis. However, this filicide would fail to meet the criteria of ICT as a deliberate and prolonged series of acts.

Sometimes organized groups participate in children’s torture. These can include cults, along with sex and labor trafficking networks. These networks often include adult family members who inflict or permit the abuse, thus qualifying as ICT. One example is Children of God (now renamed Family International), where children were routinely beaten, whipped, sexually abused, and denied education. Sex trafficking of minors involves physical and psychological torture as well as neglect, thus qualifying as ICT when family members are involved.

According to recent reports, caregivers who torture their children can be of high or low social status; related by blood or not; substance abusing or sober; of any gender; and loving or cruel to other children in the home. They are apt to keep the tortured child hidden from public view, through home or no-schooling, or networks organized around cults or crime. Learn about ICT so you can tune in to signs that children you suspect are abused may be suffering far worse: torture.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, volkswagen revealed the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, an electric pocket rocket with a massive rear wing and 362 horsepower.

We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after teasing the latest GTI hot hatch earlier this week.

Industry observers note that volkswagen debuted the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch. To celebrate the brand’s legendary performance badge, a signature of its sporty, practical hatchbacks, VW is entering a new era with its first fully electric GTI.

The GTI has been “one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years,” Volkswagen’s technical development boss, Kai Grünitz, said.

After opening pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, the brand’s first EV to wear the badge, Volkswagen introduced the Clubsport Concept, a souped-up two-door electric pocket rocket.

The fresh ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept indicates “how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world,” according to Grünitz.

In a recent development, it’s based on the production ID. Polo GTI uses the same MEB+ platform, but VW reengineered it with a larger electric motor to pump out more power.

Recent findings suggest that the Clubsport is powered by a 362 hp (270 kW) front-mounted electric motor (APP550) that’s typically used in the rear of VW’s larger EVs, like the ID. Tiguan and the ID.7. That’s up considerably from the 233 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft of torque of the standard ID. Polo GTI offers.

Thomas Schmall, CEO of Volkswagen Group Components, remarked the APP550 motor is “one of the most efficient electric drives in its class.”.

Thanks to an electronically controlled front differential lock (VAQ), Volkswagen noted, the Clubsport version can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 4.7 seconds, beating the standard ID. Polo GTI by a full two seconds (6.8 seconds).

Volkswagen also fine-tuned the adaptive chassis control (DCC) to make it racetrack-ready and added new ceramic brakes to help slow it down.

According to recent reports, the Clubsport version uses the same 52 kW NMC battery as the ID. Polo GTI, which can provide up to 389 hp (290 kW), Volkswagen mentioned, enabling a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h).

On the exterior, the Clubsport is a two-door model rather than a four-door. It’s 100 mm longer than the standard ID. Polo GTI, with each wing flared an additional 50 mm. It also gets a large motorsport splitter up front, a wider rear end, a fresh diffuser, and a massive carbon-fiber rear wing.

It has been revealed that inside, the cabin is tailored to the racetrack with a minimalist, stripped-down, two-seater layout. As such, there’s no infotainment system, just a center display to switch between drive modes.

The dash panel, side trims, and other interior elements feature dark ArtVelours microfibre with red topstitching, reinforcing the racetrack-ready interior.

Following the ID. Polo GTI, newly introduced ID.3 GTI, and Golf GTI Edition 50, the new ID. Polo Clubsport is the fourth model to debut this year under the performance badge.

Industry observers note that volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000). In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

And American compact car enthusiasts drool over more unobtanium.

It has been revealed that the company will showcase the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport concept car at the Essen Motor Show next week, starting on November 27.

Volkswagen didn’t confirm looks to launch a production version, but don’t expect it to reach the States.

Sources indicate that the standard VW ID. Polo and GTI are not sold in the US, so the souped-up Clubsport variant likely won’t be either. Hopefully, VW changes its mind and proves us wrong.

Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table.
  • It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert.
  • For generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table. The flesh has been cooked until soft. But the hard part is still ahead. To turn the pumpkin into pie, the cook must mash it, scrape it, and force it through a sieve, separating smooth pulp from stubborn strings and fibers. There is no can of pumpkin puree. No food processor. Just the pumpkin, rudimentary kitchen tools, and a lot of elbow grease. The work could take hours, all for an eight-person dessert. An 1876 Fresh England cookbook, for example, instructed cooks to simmer pumpkin for six to eight hours, stirring frequently, before rubbing it through a colander.

It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert. Pumpkin flesh doesn’t naturally break down into a silky puree. Cooking softens its tissues, but turning the squash into smooth filling requires additional mechanical work.

For generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle. Eventually, factories took over the work of cooking and processing pumpkins into puree. But the solution didn’t stop there. Growers also turned to pumpkin varieties with naturally smoother, less fibrous flesh, making the job easier before the squash even reached the factory.

Industry observers note that pumpkin was an important food in North America long before Thanksgiving became a national holiday. Indigenous peoples cultivated and prepared the squash in many forms, and European colonists adopted pumpkins as a plentiful crop. Colonists adapted their own pie-making traditions to the abundant squash, incorporating pumpkin into sweet and savory pies. By the 17th century, recipes for pumpkin-filled pies were appearing in English cookbooks.

It has been revealed that in 1796, the first known American cookbook, Amelia Simmons’s American Cookery, included a recipe for “Pompkin Pudding” made with cooked pumpkin, milk, eggs, and spices. Before the pumpkin could be combined with the other ingredients, the recipe called for it to be strained, separating fine pulp from tougher material.

Thanksgiving didn’t take shape as a national tradition until the mid-19th century. Pumpkins were harvested in the fall and could be stored through the colder months, making them a natural ingredient for a holiday associated with the autumn harvest.

The story of the Pilgrims sitting down with Native Americans for the first Thanksgiving has some truth to it, too. In 1621, English colonists and members of the Wampanoag people did gather for a three-day harvest celebration. But the friendly, feel-good version passed down in schoolbooks leaves out a much more complicated history of colonialism and conflict.

It wasn’t until over two centuries later that Sarah Josepha Hale, a prominent magazine editor, campaigned for decades for a national holiday, and, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “day of Thanksgiving.” She believed a shared day of gratitude, centered on family and community, could help unite a country increasingly divided by political conflict.

Hale also helped popularize the foods associated with the holiday, promoting a traditional Fresh England Thanksgiving menu through her magazine. Pumpkin pie was already a regional favorite, but as Thanksgiving spread nationally after the Civil War, the dessert became part of the broader American tradition.

Pumpkin pie became increasingly associated with the holiday meal during this era, drawing on its roots in Upcoming England’s seasonal cooking traditions. Preparing it remained labor-intensive, and results varied.

Sources indicate that industrial food processing offered a solution to the labor-intensive process of making pumpkin pie. Factories could cook and mechanically break down pumpkin in large quantities, producing puree without requiring every household to repeat the tedious process. Canning transformed pumpkin from a seasonal ingredient demanding considerable preparation into a convenient product that could be stored and used when needed.

John Coupland, Ph.D., professor of food science at Penn State, describes the work involved in preparing pumpkin by hand as “astonishing.” Industrial processing made pie filling far more convenient, eliminating the need to cook, mash, and strain a pumpkin from scratch.

It also gave bakers a reliable starting point, helping make pumpkin pie more consistent and cementing its place at the Thanksgiving table.

It has been revealed that making pumpkin puree is more complicated than simply cooking the flesh until soft. Pumpkin cells are surrounded by walls containing materials such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cooking softens the tissue, while mechanical processing breaks it into smaller particles. Together, these processes help determine the puree’s texture and moisture.

It has been revealed that the goal is a smooth puree that is neither watery nor full of tough fibers. The pumpkin variety matters, as do the heating conditions and mechanical methods used to break down its flesh.

According to recent reports, modern food processing allows manufacturers to control these variables on a large scale, producing batches with similar textures and moisture levels. That predictability is especially valuable in pumpkin pie, where the filling’s consistency helps determine the finished dessert.

But the food industry found another way to improve the process: start with a pumpkin better suited to the job.

That is where Libby’s, one of the country’s largest canned-pumpkin producers, and the Dickinson pumpkin enter the story.

According to recent reports, according to Libby’s, farmer Elijah Dickinson brought special Dickinson pumpkin seeds from Kentucky to Illinois in 1835. The variety became closely associated with commercial pumpkin processing, and Libby, McNeill & Libby acquired Dickinson & Co. in 1929, strengthening the tech giant’s connection to the crop.

It has been revealed that dickinson pumpkins look different from the bright orange pumpkins sold for carving (often called field pumpkins). Their tan skin matters less to processors than the dense flesh beneath it. Relatively high in solids and sugars, Dickinson pumpkins are particularly well-suited to puree.

Many carving pumpkins, by contrast, have stringier flesh that makes them harder to process into a smooth puree. Coupland explains that they are not ideally suited to commercial food production because their fibers can be difficult to break down.

Coupland describes Dickinson puree as having a “smooth, even texture,” adding that it means you won’t be “picking fibers out of your teeth.” Rather than trying to eliminate the stringiness of a carving pumpkin, processors can start with a variety whose natural characteristics make the job easier. The raw material itself becomes part of the technology.

Libby’s helped bring this approach into American kitchens through its canned-pumpkin business, pairing a suitable variety with industrial processing to deliver consistent puree to home bakers.

Industry observers note that interestingly, Dickinson pumpkins belong to Cucurbita moschata, a species that includes several varieties of winter squash. Many familiar carving pumpkins belong to Cucurbita pepo. Botanically, the distinction between pumpkin and squash is largely a matter of common usage rather than a strict scientific boundary. The FDA permits certain sweet, golden-fleshed squashes to be labeled as pumpkin in canned products, reflecting the longstanding overlap in how the terms are used in the food trade.

According to recent reports, for pumpkin pie, what matters most is the flesh inside: how it tastes, how it breaks down, and how consistently it performs. Today’s Thanksgiving cooks no longer needs to work themselves to the bone because the food industry has learned to do the work first.

Tesla FSD approved in Italy, the first big EU market to say yes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe.
  • The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.
  • It has been revealed that deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini confirmed the decision on X on Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe. Italy becomes the 12th European country to allow the system, and the first of the EU’s substantial markets.

It also didn’t wait for Brussels. The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.

It has been revealed that deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini confirmed the decision on X on Friday. He wrote that the ministry (MIT) gave the green light after a “thorough technical feasibility check,” and that Italy is getting ahead of the EU recognition process, which he described as “still being defined.”.

Tesla Europe followed with a one-liner, “Now approved in Italy, rollout begins soon,” and a video of one of its cars driving itself through Rome. There’s no firm rollout date yet.

In a recent development, it’s still a Level 2 driver-assist system. It can steer, brake, accelerate, and handle intersections and lane changes, but the driver has to supervise at all times and stays fully responsible for the car.

The Dutch vehicle authority RDW was first, approving FSD Supervised on April 10 under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation. Other member states can then recognize that approval nationally, one by one.

According to recent reports, ten did before Italy: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Those are mostly small markets. Together with the Netherlands, they add up to about 70 million people, or roughly 15% of the EU’s population.

Italy alone has about 59 million people, so Friday’s decision nearly doubles the share of Europeans who can legally use the system, to close to 30%.

Rome’s position moved fast. In April, Senator Carlo Calenda formally asked Salvini’s ministry to prioritize the approval. On October 29, Salvini posted that he’d had a “very positive and constructive” call with Elon Musk and that Italy supported a “swift EU approval,” which read at the time as backing for an EU-level decision, not a national one. Three weeks later, Italy went national.

A lot changed in between. Tesla dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe after Germany’s Transport Ministry called it misleading, and cut the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit. Then on November 16, the RDW approved stricter driver monitoring, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h. That’s the version Italy is approving.

In a recent development, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) pushed the Tesla vote to December after holding only discussions in October. Bloc-wide approval needs a qualified majority: at least 15 of 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Recent findings suggest that germany stated in October it would back approval after Tesla agreed to the rename and the speed cap. If it follows through, Germany and the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of the EU’s population.

That’s progress for Tesla, but it’s not 65%. France refused a national approval in July, and Spain hasn’t recognized the Dutch approval. Tesla needs at least one of them, plus most of the remaining holdouts.

I used FSD for five days this past week. It's impressive on controlled roads.

Even in Chill driving mode, there were still more than a few times that I had to use the Critical feedback.

Tech Report: Mind Games: My ‘Secret’ to Enjoying Coffee Without Anxiety

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.
  • According to recent reports, my morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.

Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.

According to recent reports, my morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m. if I drink it past noon. As an already anxious human, the last thing I need is to exacerbate my symptoms, even if it’s coming from a delicious source.

It has been revealed that over a year ago, I noticed that my anxiety was higher than usual. I was also tossing and turning and waking up at all hours of the night for weeks on end.

In a recent development, one night in particular, I woke up every hour for 8 hours. Naturally, I wanted to blame it on the full moon or anything other than my beloved coffee, but alas, I realized that my caffeine consumption was the most likely culprit.

Could I have aimed to set a strict drinking schedule to see if that fixed things? Sure. But instead, I decided to quit cold turkey and undergo an experiment to see how I’d feel going coffee-free for the first time in years.

It has been revealed that over the next 8 months, I’d swap my coffee station for a matcha setup, dabble in exotic herbal blends from my local teahouse, and become a self-proclaimed tea connoisseur. Lo and behold, my anxiety eased up, and my sleep quality improved, too.

In a recent development, fast forward to 4 months ago, when I hopped back on the coffee train. But this time, I’m relying on a handy amino acid to help avoid anxiety and other unwanted side effects: L-theanine.

Health and wellness touch everyone’s life differently. This is one person’s story. The views and opinions expressed are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Healthline Media and should not serve as a substitute for medical advice from a healthcare professional.

It has been revealed that L-theanine is mainly found in green and black tea and one type of wild mushroom. The mental health benefits of L-theanine consumption are an emerging area of research, but one 2024 review found that consuming around 200 to 400 milligrams (mg) may help relieve symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

Still, anecdotal reports suggest there may be benefits of adding L-theanine to coffee. Over the last 5 years, the combo has been gaining traction on Reddit and TikTok for managing caffeine-related side effects.

Despite an overwhelming amount of rave reviews online, I couldn’t find much research to support these claims, so I spoke with a neurologist to see if they had any thoughts.

“This trend has real science behind it,” said Fawad Mian, MD, who is board certified in neurology, clinical neurophysiology, and sleep medicine and the founder of Ascend Regenerative.

It has been revealed that “Controlled studies show caffeine plus L-theanine improves focus and attention more than caffeine alone, and some suggest it softens caffeine’s side effects, like tiredness, headaches, and blood pressure spikes,” Mian said. “It smooths caffeine’s effects but doesn’t erase them, so it’s not a license to drink more coffee,” he added.

With all of this in mind, especially after realizing just how calm I was while drinking black and green teas during my coffee break, I decided to give it a try.

After about 4 months of “testing,” I’ve found that adding L-theanine to my coffee works extremely well for me.

No more anxiety, scatterbrain, shakiness, or staying up until 3 a.m. And no lifestyle overhaul needed. The supplement, which I prefer in liquid form, has become a seamless addition to my daily routine.

Every morning, I make a fresh batch of French press coffee with (strong) local beans, then I squeeze some L-theanine into my cup.

I’ve noticed that I get the usual coffee benefits like improved focus and concentration, plus a nice, calm, stable energy throughout the day.

Even if I drink it until 2 p.m., I’m fighting to keep my eyes open at night before I finally fall asleep around 10. Perhaps this is because L-theanine may also support quality sleep.

Mindful L-Theanine Drops is the liquid supplement that I use every day.

I add a one-second squeeze (which contains 200 mg of L-theanine) into my morning coffee, then I’m good to go. I even started carrying a bottle in my bag just in case I get a latte from a coffee shop on a whim.

You can also add it to a glass of water, a cup of tea, or another drink of your choosing. It’s unflavored, so it doesn’t alter the taste of your drinks. Real secret stuff.

Out of curiosity, and because I’m a natural skeptic and overthinker, I asked Mian if my positive experience could be a placebo effect, or if I’m seeing real results.

According to recent reports, “Expectation may play a small role, but the effect is biologically plausible,” he noted. “L-theanine boosts calming brain activity that offsets caffeine’s stimulation, and 200 mg matches the doses used in studies.” However, he noted that it doesn’t speed caffeine clearance, so drinking coffee only in the morning still matters for sleep quality.

While L-theanine is generally safe to consume, it’s best to speak with a healthcare professional first, especially if you’re pregnant, nursing, receiving cancer treatment, or taking blood pressure medication or sedatives.

“Choose a third-party tested brand, and if caffeine makes you anxious, cutting back is still the simplest fix,” Mian added.

Recent findings suggest that so, if you’re anything like me and drinking coffee also leads to anxiety and jitters for you, I highly recommend trying this supplement once you get the green light from your doctor. It’s been working for me. It may work well for you, too.

💌 Over to you: I’d love to hear your thoughts on this. Does coffee also give you unwanted side effects? Have you tried L-theanine to remedy them? Let me know, or ask any questions about my experience by emailing me here.
